notes.meaning: Eliphaz starts the second round of speeches between Job and his friends. Instead of being softened by Job's deep pain, he attacks Job's words even more sharply than before. He insists that Job's attitude shows a lack of true wisdom and respect for God.

Eliphaz asks whether a truly wise person would give empty arguments. He compares Job's speeches to the scorching east wind from the desert, which is violent, dry, and destructive. In his view, Job is simply blowing hot air that helps nobody.

Eliphaz continues his rebuke by asking whether anyone should argue with useless talk. He believes Job has spoken many words without providing any real sense or solid proof. Such speeches do no good for the speaker, the listeners, or the honor of God.

Eliphaz charges Job with tearing down the fear of God and hindering prayer. He thinks that Job's claim—that God treats the good and the bad the same way—will convince people that praying is useless. He assumes that Job has given up humble, reverent meditation before his Maker.

Eliphaz tells Job that his own sin is guiding what he says. He accuses Job of talking like the crafty serpent in the garden of Eden, using clever words to hide an impious heart. Job's smooth language looks to Eliphaz like an attempt to blame God while excusing himself.

Eliphaz declares that Job has already lost his case without anyone else needing to testify. The bitter and irreverent complaints Job has spoken are enough to convict him of wickedness. By speaking so boldly against God's providence, Job has become his own worst accuser.

Eliphaz uses biting sarcasm, asking if Job was the very first human ever created. He asks if Job existed before the ancient mountains were shaped. If Job was not present at the beginning of the world, he has no right to claim superior insight into how God runs it.

Eliphaz asks whether Job was invited into God's secret heavenly council. He demands to know if Job thinks he has locked up all wisdom for himself alone. Humans cannot know God's hidden plans unless the Lord reveals them, and Eliphaz thinks Job is acting far too proud.

Eliphaz turns Job's earlier words back on him, asking what Job could possibly understand that the friends do not already know. He refuses to grant that Job has any higher spiritual knowledge. In Eliphaz's eyes, the friends have weighed every fact just as carefully as Job has.

Eliphaz points to the great age and experience on their side of the debate. He claims that their view of God's justice is supported by venerable elders who are even older than Job's father. In the ancient world, advanced age was treated as the surest source of reliable wisdom.

Eliphaz asks why Job treats divine consolations as something small and worthless. He views the promises of restoration that the friends offered—if Job would only repent—as gentle words sent from God Himself. By brushing off their advice, Job seems to be rejecting God's own comfort.

Eliphaz asks why Job allows his emotions and pride to carry him away. He wonders why Job's eyes flash with disdain and anger while his friends are speaking. An uncontrolled temper leads people away from calm, humble reflection before God.

Eliphaz accuses Job of directing his angry spirit straight at the Almighty. He cannot understand how a godly man could let such challenging, defiant words spill out of his mouth. In the eyes of the friends, venting frustration toward heaven is a mark of open rebellion.

Eliphaz asks how any frail mortal could ever claim to be clean and righteous before God. Every person born into this world inherits weakness and sinfulness from birth. Since all humans are flawed, Eliphaz thinks Job's defense of his own innocence is completely absurd.

Eliphaz reminds Job that God does not even place absolute trust in the holy angels. Compared to the pure holiness of the Creator, even the spotless heavens seem flawed. If heavenly beings fall short of God's perfection, human beings have no room to boast.

If holy angels are imperfect before God, corrupt human beings are far worse. Eliphaz describes mankind as drinking down wickedness as eagerly and naturally as a thirsty person gulps water. He aims this harsh description directly at Job, assuming Job's suffering reveals hidden guilt.

differ.view: Human beings are totally depraved and polluted by original sin from birth, so that only the cleansing blood of Jesus Christ can make anyone pure.
This verse describes the bad man who greedily thirsts after evil, unlike the righteous person whose heart hungers and thirsts for holiness.

notes.meaning: Eliphaz asks Job to listen attentively while he lays out the facts. He promises to speak from real life and share what he has seen with his own eyes. Personal experience and careful observation, he argues, confirm that God always punishes the wicked.

Eliphaz says that his message is not an invention of his own, but comes from wise sages of old. These ancient thinkers received the truth from their ancestors and passed it down faithfully. Truth about God's justice is valuable because it has stood the test of generations.

Eliphaz notes that these ancient fathers lived in a peaceful land untouched by foreign invasions. Because no strangers came in to dilute their culture or religion, their spiritual tradition remained pure. He suggests that their undisturbed history gives their sayings special authority.

Eliphaz states his core doctrine: a wicked person suffers inward agony all the days of his life. Even when an oppressor seems powerful, he lives under the constant fear of sudden death. His cruelty to others deprives him of any true peace of mind.

The sinner is haunted by scary noises and constant alarms in his own mind. Even while he is enjoying prosperity and safety, a guilty conscience makes him fear that an enemy will ruin him. Guilt turns a man's imagination into a place of never-ending dread.

When trouble falls on the wicked man, he has no hope of ever climbing back out of the darkness. His conscience tells him that he is marked for violent death by the sword. Unlike a believer who expects light after darkness, the guilty oppressor expects only judgment.

Eliphaz paints a grim picture of the wicked man reduced to begging and searching for a scrap of bread. He knows in his heart that a day of utter ruin has arrived and cannot be stopped. The oppressor who once feasted in luxury now faces total want and doom.

Anxiety and deep sorrow terrify the sinner and break through all his defenses. These inner terrors overpower him just like a king marching to battle with an irresistible army. A troubled conscience brings an inward misery that no amount of wealth can hold back.

Eliphaz explains why the wicked man meets such misery: he raised his hand in open defiance against God. In his proud moments of power, he acted like a mighty ruler who could challenge the Almighty Himself. Rebelling against the Creator is the height of human madness.

The sinner stubbornly rushes forward like an arrogant warrior charging straight at God. He hides behind his thick, studded shield, acting as if human armor could protect him from the Lord. It is completely futile to run against the Maker of heaven and earth.

Eliphaz describes the rebel as someone who has grown sleek and heavy from years of luxury. His face and body are covered with fat, showing how completely he pampered his physical desires. Living only for bodily pleasure hardened his heart and blinded him to God's judgments.

The oppressor settles down in ruined towns and abandoned homes that were destined for destruction. Whether he made them desolate by war or built on cursed sites, his pride cannot save them. Places marked by God's judgment will end up as heaps of rubble regardless of human effort.

The tyrant's wealth will dry up and will not last. His ill-gotten gains will vanish, and his grand estates will not spread across the countryside. Possessions gained through violence and fraud carry God's curse and soon disappear.

The wicked man will never break free from the darkness of God's judgment. Divine wrath will scorch his branches, meaning his children and wealth, like a hot desert flame. In the end, a single breath from God's mouth will carry him away into ruin.

Eliphaz warns people not to deceive themselves by trusting in worthless, empty things. Anyone who relies on sin or temporary wealth will receive only emptiness as his payout. Leaning on deceitful treasures always leaves a person empty-handed in the day of trouble.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Even if a man has trusted in vanity, he can still escape total ruin if he repents of his sins and turns back to God.

notes.meaning: The sinner's life and prosperity will be cut short before his natural time is up. His family line and honors will wither like a tree whose branches lose their green freshness. Unfaithfulness to God leaves a household stripped and desolate.

Eliphaz compares the wicked man to a grapevine that drops its unripe fruit, or an olive tree that sheds its blossoms. All his big plans, along with the hopes he placed in his children, will fail before reaching maturity. Sin robs a person's life of its promised fruit.

The household and companions of the godless will become completely barren. Divine fire will burn down the dwellings that were built or enriched through bribes. Eliphaz is dropping a sharp hint that Job's ruined home and lost children were signs of hidden dishonesty.

Eliphaz wraps up his speech by saying that the wicked conceive trouble and give birth to evil. Their deepest thoughts are constantly hatching schemes to deceive and exploit others. In the end, the deceit they nurture inside themselves brings about their own destruction.
